enrichment.short_title: Confiscation benefit after revenue fraud on company income
key_facts: John Foggon diverted about £1 million of Vaclensa customer receipts into a concealed TSB account and used the money largely for private purposes without declaring it for tax.
He pleaded guilty to cheating the public revenue and was sentenced to two years' imprisonment; a confiscation order of £1,068,441 was made.
The prosecution accepted that unamended CJA 1988 provisions applied because the offence predated POCA 1995 amendments.
Foggon argued benefit should be measured as unpaid corporation tax under section 71(5), not as diverted property under section 71(4).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against a Crown Court confiscation order following conviction for cheating the public revenue.
enrichment.ratio: Where a director misappropriates company money as an essential part of a fraud on the Revenue, the misappropriated sums are property obtained in connection with the offence under section 71(4) CJA 1988; unpaid corporation tax owed by the company is not the offender's pecuniary advantage under section 71(5) unless the tax was his own liability or corporate veil piercing applies.
legal_issues: Whether POCA 1995 amendments or unamended CJA 1988 governed the confiscation order
Whether benefit was diverted property under section 71(4) or unpaid tax under section 71(5)
Whether a post-discovery VAT payment should reduce the confiscation figure

confidence.notes: Outcome, statutory analysis, and benefit measure are clearly resolved in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Registered homes tribunal reasons on care home fitness
key_facts: W owned three registered residential care homes near Exeter for residents with learning disabilities and mental health needs.
Devon County Council proposed cancelling her registration on grounds including intimidation of residents and staff, unprofessional conduct, failure to report a serious incident, and NVQ plagiarism.
After an 11-day hearing the Registered Homes Tribunal dismissed her appeal and found she was not a fit person to run the homes.
W appealed to the High Court arguing the tribunal's reasons were inadequately expressed on multiple findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 11 Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 from a Registered Homes Tribunal decision cancelling registration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A registered homes tribunal must give proper reasons enabling the losing party to understand why they lost, including summary basic findings of fact where necessary, but need not recite every evidential dispute or reject every unpersuasive argument; specialist tribunals may express findings concisely where the decision is comprehensible on the evidence.
legal_issues: Whether tribunal reasons were sufficiently intelligible
Adequacy of findings on intimidation, restraint, and professional conduct
Treatment of hearsay and credibility of former staff and residents
Whether irrelevant historical complaints influenced the decision
linked_authorities: Elliott and others v Southwark Borough Council
Meek v City of Birmingham District Council

confidence.notes: Core procedural-law ratio and outcome are clear. Source judge metadata lists cited authorities rather than the hearing judge; Mackay J delivered the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Unfair dismissal remedies and late fraud allegation
key_facts: Felicia Panama, a Hackney housing officer on job share, was suspended after solicitors' letters of 28 May 1998 appeared to show a conflict of interest with her employer.
Hackney dismissed her with pay in lieu of notice before a scheduled disciplinary hearing; the tribunal found the dismissal procedurally unfair.

At remedies hearing the tribunal held she would probably have been summarily dismissed for gross misconduct if disciplinary proceedings had continued, based on a late fraud allegation arising in cross-examination.
The allegation relied on a Caprice report suggesting a tenant had been advised to fabricate claims about brain-damaged children.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employee appeal to the Court of Appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of appeals against employment tribunal liability and remedies decisions.
enrichment.ratio: A serious dishonesty allegation must be pleaded with sufficient formality and early enough for the employee to answer it; where a tribunal hypothetically finds summary dismissal for fraud would have followed, it must apply section 98 ERA 1996 and Burchell reasonableness, including whether the employer had reasonable grounds and carried out adequate investigation.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal erred in finding hypothetical gross misconduct dismissal
Fairness of raising fraud for the first time in cross-examination
Application of Burchell test to hypothetical disciplinary outcome
Adequacy of investigation into authorship of solicitors' letters
linked_authorities: British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell

confidence.notes: Court of Appeal clearly allowed the appeal on procedural fairness and Burchell grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal missed through solicitor notification failure
key_facts: Hasa, a Kosovan ethnic Albanian asylum seeker, missed her adjudicator hearing because her new solicitors notified the Home Office Appeals Support Section but not the Immigration Appellate Authority of their instruction.
The adjudicator dismissed her appeal in her absence, finding credibility could not be tested.
She suffered domestic violence from her husband and had a non-molestation order; her case had not been heard on merits.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal as out of time; she was removed to Kosovo shortly after solicitors gave pre-action notice of judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of leave to appeal and of the Secretary of State's removal of the claimant.
enrichment.outcome: IAT refusal of leave quashed; removal challenge dismissed; leave to appeal granted to the Secretary of State.
enrichment.ratio: Where special circumstances include denial of any effective asylum hearing through a chain of administrative and professional errors rather than the claimant's fault, an Immigration Appeal Tribunal must consider whether extension of time and leave to appeal are justified; notifying the Home Office alone does not satisfy Rule 47 address-for-service duties to the appellate authority.
legal_issues: Whether IAT refusal of leave was judicially reviewable
Whether solicitor error should be treated as claimant error
Application of Rule 18 special circumstances for extension of time
Lawfulness of removal after pre-action correspondence
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Hannach
Lapido v Secretary of State for the Home Department
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Asifa Salim
Al-Mehdawi v Secretary of State for the Home Department
R on the application of Tewedros Tadesse Haile v Immigration Appeal Tribunal

confidence.notes: Split outcome on the two JR limbs and the quashing of the IAT decision are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Section 42 vexatious litigant all proceedings order
key_facts: Mr Badibanga had brought about 20 civil actions, four criminal prosecutions, and numerous applications since the early 1990s, nearly all unsuccessful.
Litigation stemmed from a failed property dispute with the Mayhews and Barclays Bank and expanded to repeated claims against officials and institutions.
Claims were repeatedly struck out as vexatious or disclosing no cause of action; Grepe v Loam orders were breached.
The Solicitor General applied for an all proceedings order under section 42.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General application for a section 42 Supreme Court Act 1981 all proceedings order against a habitual litigant.
enrichment.ratio: An all proceedings order under section 42 may be made where a person habitually and persistently institutes vexatious proceedings without reasonable ground, including by relitigating the same causes, automatically appealing adverse decisions, and disregarding court orders; prior court findings of vexatiousness cannot be reopened on such an application.
legal_issues: Whether Badibanga's litigation was habitual and persistent
Whether proceedings were vexatious and without reasonable ground
Whether prior strike-out decisions could be relitigated
Appropriate scope of an all proceedings order

confidence.notes: Order granted and legal test clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Council tax disaggregation of elderly bedsits

statutes_considered.title: Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) Regulations 1993

key_facts: Eleven elderly residents' bedsits at Ty Gnoll, Neath each had a front door, bedroom/living space, kitchen, and WC with wash basin; bathing was shared.
The valuation officer listed each bedsit separately; Age Concern argued they were not self-contained units.
The valuation tribunal aggregated the bedsits as one band F dwelling, citing insufficient washing facilities, communality, and single access.
Residents and the tribunal did not oppose the listing officer's statutory appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under regulation 32 of the 1993 Regulations against a valuation tribunal decision on council tax listing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal decision set aside and listing restored with separate entries.
enrichment.ratio: Whether accommodation is a self-contained unit under Article 2 of the 1992 Order depends on how it was constructed or adapted for separate living, not on occupiers' age or communal facilities; absence of a bath or shower does not prevent disaggregation, and market saleability or degree of communality are irrelevant.
legal_issues: Definition of self-contained unit under Article 2
Relevance of shared bathing and communal facilities
Whether elderly occupiers' needs affect the construction test
Whether single building access prevents disaggregation
index_terms: R v London South East Valuation Tribunal ex parte Moore
linked_authorities: R v London South East Valuation Tribunal and Neale ex parte Moore
Beasley Listing Officer v National Council of YMCAs

confidence.notes: Four legal errors and direct remedial order are clearly identified.

enrichment.short_title: Section 86 extended licence and Article 7 ECHR
key_facts: JT was convicted of indecent assault and gross indecency against three young granddaughters between July 1981 and November 1988.
He received concurrent sentences totalling two and a half years' imprisonment.
The judge purported to extend the licence period under section 86 PCC(S)A 2000 for the whole sentence to ensure post-release supervision.
Section 86 applies only where part of the sentence was imposed for a sexual offence committed before 30 September 1998.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against extension of licence period under section 86 following conviction for historical child sex offences.
enrichment.outcome: Section 86 extension quashed; custodial term otherwise unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: Extended licence under section 86 is punitive and, read compatibly with Article 7 ECHR via section 3 HRA 1998, has no effect for offences committed before 1 October 1992 when no equivalent whole-sentence supervision power existed.
legal_issues: Whether section 86 creates a heavier penalty for pre-1992 offences
Application of Article 7 and section 3 HRA 1998
Whether extended licence is punitive or preventative
Retrospectivity of section 44 CJA 1991 / section 86 PCC(S)A 2000

confidence.notes: Appeal outcome and statutory interpretation are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Manual handling policy for profoundly disabled sisters

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970
National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: Sisters A and B, profoundly physically and learning disabled adults, were cared for at home by their mother and stepfather with support from East Sussex County Council.
The council adopted manual handling policies limiting manual lifting; the Disability Rights Commission supported the claimants.
Claimants sought to quash September 2001 assessments, declare a blanket no-manual-lifting policy unlawful, and require care under earlier care plans.
Munby J held the judicial review was premature because ESCC had not completed revised risk assessments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of local authority manual handling assessments and care plans, with the Disability Rights Commission as interested party.
enrichment.outcome: Full mandatory and quashing relief not granted at this stage; court set out legal principles and directed ESCC to complete assessments, with scope for further challenge.
enrichment.ratio: Manual handling policy for disabled people must balance article 8 dignity of the service user against carers' health and safety; blanket bans on manual lifting are unlikely lawful, but the primary decision-maker is the local authority and the court's role is review, not to draft care protocols or make primary assessments.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of blanket no-manual-lifting policies
Balance between Article 8 rights and manual handling regulations
Whether the court could order specific care plans
Prematurity of challenge before completed assessments
Margin of appreciation in community care decisions
linked_authorities: R (Daly) v Secretary of State for the Home Department
R (Mahmood) v Secretary of State for the Home Department

confidence.notes: Long judgment focused on legal principles rather than final quashing relief; outcome reflects interim/prematurity reasoning at paragraphs 165-166.

enrichment.short_title: ATE premium percentage of damages not champertous
key_facts: Pirie accepted a £13,000 Part 36 payment in a road traffic personal injury claim.
She claimed recovery of a £2,600 after-the-event insurance premium calculated as 20% of damages under a Costs Support policy.
The defendant argued the premium agreement was champertous and in any event unreasonable.
The court allowed only £367.50 including IPT, comparing to Callery v Gray levels.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Assessment of recoverable ATE insurance premium following acceptance of a Part 36 offer in county court proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Premium recoverable in principle but reduced from £2,600 to £367.50.
enrichment.ratio: An ATE premium calculated as a percentage of damages is not champertous where the insurer bears litigation risk and does not divide litigation spoils; under section 29 AJA 1999 the paying party must pay a reasonable and proportionate premium, and a flat percentage of damages is inherently unreasonable in simple road accident cases.
legal_issues: Whether percentage-of-damages ATE premium is champertous
Reasonableness and proportionality under section 29
Comparison with conditional fee success fees
Quantum of recoverable premium
index_terms: R (Factortame) v Secretary of State for Transport
linked_authorities: R (Factortame) v Secretary of State for Transport

confidence.notes: Short costs judgment with clear holdings on champerty and quantum.

enrichment.short_title: Interim costs payment after patent inquiry settlement
key_facts: Dyson succeeded against Hoover for infringement of a cyclone vacuum cleaner patent and elected for an inquiry as to damages.
Dyson claimed over £21 million but accepted a £4 million payment in shortly before a two-week inquiry hearing.
Dyson sought an interim costs payment of about £1.2-1.4 million on account of over £2.5 million inquiry preparation costs.
Hoover argued proportionality and that the judge, who had not heard the inquiry, should not order interim payment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for interim payment on account of costs under CPR 44.3.8 after settlement of a patent damages inquiry.
enrichment.ratio: Where a judge has not heard the trial or inquiry, there is no presumption in favour of interim costs payment under CPR 44.3.8; the court must decide on merits, and without sufficient information a large interim payment would be speculative and achieve little toward settlement when proportionality disputes remain for the costs judge.
legal_issues: Whether Mars UK v Teknowledge presumption applies without full trial
Interaction of CPR 44.3.8 and CPR 47.15 interim certificates
Effect of late commencement of detailed assessment
Proportionality of inquiry costs relative to damages recovered
linked_authorities: Mars UK Limited v Teknowledge Limited

confidence.notes: Application refused with detailed reasoning distinguishing Mars where the trial judge had heard the case.
